header.source: Translated by Claude (claude-opus-5-5, Anthropic) from the library's tmp221.tmp221.opp-lat1, from Open Greek and Latin's Patrologia Latina (CC BY-SA 4.0), one English line for each line of the original. The whole work is translated. It was chosen because no English translation of it could be found.
header.statement: An AI-generated translation of the whole work, checked against the original by a second AI only in samples. No specialist has reviewed it.

Stray letters (a, b, c, etc.) are footnote marks from the printed edition and have been omitted. In 1, 'nonnulli' may be corrupt (perhaps for an epithet of the brothers). In 3, 'mίπαγομένονς' is read as Greek ἐπαγομένους (epagomenai). In 6, 'quarta decima dodran' is taken as 'fourteen and three-quarters' (dodrans = three-quarters), that is, the moon's age at creation; the reading is uncertain. Also in 6, the sentence 'Eo enim tempore lunam talem mane quod oritur, sol respicit in Occidentem...' is syntactically disordered, and the translation gives the probable sense. The question in 1 ('Cur ergo hodie...') is left incomplete in the Latin.

Section IX: 'CCCLIII' (353) is printed where the argument requires 354; probably a corruption. The syntax of the list of the eleven days ('Sex dies cavaturarum...') is loose and has been rendered as a continuation of the preceding sentence. Section X is obscurely worded; the sense of 'incrementa assis... ortum ad nativitatem debere tenere' is uncertain. Section XII: the text speaks of 'XXVIII dies' though it earlier gives twenty-nine, and the three ranges listed (11 + 8 + 10) total twenty-nine. The ranges are also inconsistent with the Roman calendar as printed (e.g. 'the third before the Nones of April' for the end of the last range, where the earlier limit was the fourth). 'Mensis novorum' is rendered literally as 'month of new things'. 'Phasec' is a transliteration of the Hebrew for Passover. Scanning errors corrected silently (e.g. 'primiidedicabis', 'inXIVmensis', 'filiifIsrael', 'adhvesperam').

XIII: the edition prints 'DCLXX' (670) for five times 354; the arithmetic and the total (2922) require 1770 (MDCCLXX), so 1770 is translated. The stray letters a, b after the numbers are footnote marks. 'congregavit' in the last sentence is taken as 'came together/agreed'. 'Pascha' is rendered 'Pascha' in XIV–XV, where the author contrasts the Christian and Jewish feasts. XV: the closing sentence lacks a finite verb until 'celebramus'; the participle 'retinentes' and the preceding phrases are construed with it. The dates are 3 March 397 (the consulship of Caesarius and Atticus, i.e. the year after the fourth consulship of Arcadius and the third of Honorius).

nodes.text: THE TREATISE OF QUINTUS JULIUS HILARIANUS ON THE DAY OF EASTER AND THE MONTH.

I. Brothers, some [of us], servants of God, have often come together to discuss certain matters from the divine Scriptures. There, at their request, I spoke briefly for the time being about the PASCHAL CYCLE and promised that I would set out a full account. So the brothers' bidding has reminded me of my promise again and often: that what we discussed some time ago, gradually and patiently, about the reckoning of Easter should now be settled in writing by me. The question is this. The Lord God named to Moses nothing other than the first month, and commanded that Easter be celebrated in it, saying: This month [shall be] the beginning of months; it shall be first for you among the months of the year. Speak therefore to the whole congregation of the children of Israel, that they keep the Passover, beginning from the fourteenth of this month at evening until the twenty-first (Exod. 12:2, 3, 18, according to the Septuagint). But divine Scripture has not declared to us with a fully evident answer where this first month begins or where it has its end. Why then do we today look for the first moon from the third day before the Nones of March to the fourth day before the Nones of April? Or why is it confirmed from the fifteenth day before the Kalends of April to the seventeenth day before the Kalends of May that it is the fourteenth [moon]? Thereafter, wherever the day of Easter falls, we celebrate it lawfully, as we know it was celebrated and handed down by our Fathers. Now the time has come for us, in my discourse, to go through everything in order according to the reckoning of the Law. We hold, namely, that Easter was commanded to be celebrated not from the beginning of the world but from Moses, by the sacred voice; and that the first month does not begin as the Egyptians begin their first month, from the fourth day before the Kalends of September, or as the Romans do, from the Kalends of January, but that by the authority of the divine Law the moon, in its course, always and every year produces the first month for us. But in order that we may know this first month lawfully for the sake of our Easter, we are compelled by sure reasoning to go back to the origin of the world, so that we may know the day on which the lights were made, and what kind of moon God made for the world; although in the construction of the world nothing else is to be believed than that almighty God established all things equal, full and perfect.

II. First, then, it must be shown which day it was, when the fabric of the world was begun, that almighty God established by creating light. Second, we shall show what kind of moon was made by God at evening, and where its year comes to an end. Then we shall explain why we look for the first moon from the third day before the Nones of March to the fourth day before the Nones of April, and why, for the complete celebration of Easter, the fourteenth [moon] is required from the fifteenth day before the Kalends of April to the seventeenth day before the Kalends of May; so that every way of approach may be closed to those who are eager to contradict, and they may not think that we have defined the reckoning insufficiently in any respect.

III. When the Law had not yet been given by the almighty Lord, people often hesitated over the course of the moon. Some called the full orb, such as it had arisen for the world at God's command, the first [day]; others thought otherwise. So, counting the months only by the number thirty, they completed the course of twelve months in three hundred and sixty days, just as the Scripture of Genesis shows that, at the time of the Flood, thirty days ran in a month. The five days, that is, which remain to complete the year were called empty, in memory of God's work of making. For the world was made in five days, and man was made on the sixth day after all things; and from that day, to run through twelve months, his count of days was three hundred and sixty, up to the day before the day which God established first. Then there were five empty days up to the day before the birthday of that same man who was first formed. From this custom or tradition it is known to have remained among certain peoples, as among the Egyptians, who keep these five empty days and call them *epagomenai* ['added days']. And by some Roman writers who wished to write on the reckoning of days they were called black and intercalary [days]. So in ancient times no one, since God had not yet shown the course of the sun and moon, no one among men grasped the seasons of spring and summer or the bounds of autumn and winter, or gathered the increases and decreases of days and nights, which these lights were commanded by God's order to unfold in their own times until the end of time. Hence almighty God, for the time [being], among many words of reproof, admonished even that most holy and most blessed Job about this, saying: And tell me this, whether you know the course of the sun and moon (Job 28:19)? For at the time when we know the Law was given to Moses by the Lord our God for the celebration of Easter, He handed down to him the reckoning of months and years by the course of the moon, so that from the new moon he could have the first month and the others. This is now gathered from the tradition of the Law, provided that whoever wishes to gather it examines it most carefully. Applying ourselves to this matter, we set out each point, beginning, as we said, from the first day of the world.

IV. In the beginning, says Moses, God made heaven and earth. But the earth was invisible and unformed, and darkness was over the abyss, and the Spirit of God was borne over the waters. And God said, Let there be light, and there was light. And God saw the light, that it was good, and God divided between the light and the darkness. And God called the light day, and the darkness He called night. And there was evening, and there was morning, one day. And God divided between the light and the darkness, that is, He balanced day and night (Gen. 1:1–5, according to the Septuagint). For light, made at God's command, so cut through the darkness that the course between the two appeared equal, and from then on day and night received increases and decreases in turn, and showed the seasons. For just as almighty God commanded the earth and the seas to bring forth every living creature, first in full maturity according to its kind, and also all the fruits of the earth at once, perfect with their seeds, so He first of all established the extent of light and darkness in an equal course. This, then, is known to be the first day, which was made at the origin, on which the Lord God made light and night equal, namely in springtime, which almighty God willed to be the head of the year.

V. At that time, then, He also made the world. For before all times the Lord deigned to establish this season first, since it is gentle above the others, balanced in the quality of its air; in it all things that spring from the earth, the numbness of icy winter being over and this glad air of spring received, burst forth into various flowers and seeds of different kinds, so that they too, in a way, may join in celebrating the praises of the Lord Creator with the fruitful first-fruits, together with the festivals of men, in a most welcome fertility of sweetness. In it also, even now, falls the first equinox instituted by the Lord, which according to the naming of the Roman months is found on the eighth day before the Kalends of April. Taking our start from here, therefore, we shall run through all that we have proposed.

VI. We have spoken briefly about the first day of the world and explained it. Now let us come to the reckoning of the moon. When three days had passed, on the fourth day, that is, the fifth day before the Kalends of April, the lights were established for signs and seasons, days and years, but not at the same time. For although they were made on one day, almighty God, to make the day bright for us, established the sun in the morning. Then, as night approached, He instituted the monthly moon, turning in a varied course into numbers and seasons. This moon was made at evening fourteen and three-quarters [days old], for this reason: that it might light up all the darkness of the first night and run through the whole night, and that on the sixth day, for the new man for whom the Lord God was making these things, just as the sun had already been made for the day, so the moon, advancing for the night, might seem to come forth as another work for him, lest, abandoned at the departure of light and the brightness of the sun, he should suffer unexpected and lonely darkness. For at that time, as the sun rises in the morning, it looks upon such a moon in the west; and at the beginning of night, after the departure of light and the completed course of the sun, the moon comes forth shield-round with the strength of its light. Not without reason, also, did the Lord God through Moses in Exodus command His people that Easter should be celebrated from the fourteenth moon of the first month, full at evening, until the twenty-first. For the Lord willed the week of Easter to begin from the fourteenth, full at evening, so that, as the day of Easter dawned, which is the first of that same week, the fifteenth moon would be for them the first day of unleavened bread. For the Lord declares this in Leviticus, saying: In the first month, on the fourteenth day of the month, between the evenings, [is] the Passover to the Lord, and on the fifteenth of this month the festival day of unleavened bread to the Lord (Lev. 23:5, 6, according to the Septuagint). For lunar days begin at evening and end at evening, since the moon, so that by its light it might temper the darkness of night for man who was still new, took its rise from the evening of the fifth day before the Kalends of April, the day of its birth, and until the next evening, that is, the fourth day before the Kalends of April, it showed the course of its first day. Therefore today, taught the lunar course by God, we keep the vigil of Easter and celebrate it as evening begins.

VII. We have set out what the moon was like when it was made by the Lord on the fifth day before the Kalends of April, at evening. Now we also show where it completed its year. For this year set the limit for the other years. But that the moon, as we mentioned above, would show months and years by its course through the new moons, that is, the new and first days of the months, which the moon brings forth, the Lord God declares by His own testimony. For so it is written: And the Lord God spoke to Moses, saying: On the first day of the new moon of the first month you shall dedicate the tabernacle of witness (Exod. 40:1, 2, according to the Septuagint). And in another place, when He speaks of sacrifices, when and how they ought to be offered, He says: You shall also offer sacrifices, and at the new moons of the month, from month to month through the months of the year (Num. 28:11, 14, according to the Septuagint). In the book of Kingdoms it is also said: When David was hiding, fearing King Saul, the new moon came, and the king went in to the table to eat, and the usual guests came with him. But David did not go in with him, and his place was seen [empty], and Saul said nothing that day; and it happened on the morrow, on the second day of the month (1 Kgs 20:24–26, according to the Septuagint). In the Psalms also it is said: God set the moon for seasons (Ps. 103:19). The moon therefore completes a month in twenty-nine and a half days. Why? Because it does not end with its light wholly thinned away. Otherwise it would now be a different work, not that which almighty God had first made. The thirtieth moon, then, lying hidden, is hollowed in the half [day]. Twelve times twenty-nine and a half, therefore, make three hundred and fifty-four days. VIII. And so on the fifth day before the Nones of March that same moon completed its year in its running. We can prove this through the individual months of that moon's year. For this moon completed its first month on the second day before the Ides of April, because God made it full for the world and commanded it to go forth.
It completed its second month on the fourth day before the Ides of May.
Its third month it completed on the third day before the Ides of June.

Its fourth month on the sixth day before the Ides of July. Its fifth month on the fifth day before the Ides of August. Its sixth month on the seventh day before the Ides of September. Its seventh month on the Nones of October. Its eighth month on the Nones of November. Its ninth month on the Nones of December. Its tenth month on the third day before the Nones of January. Its eleventh month on the fourth day before the Nones of February. Its twelfth month, indeed, it assigned to the fifth day before the Nones of March; and on the fourth day before the Nones of March, after the fifth day before those same Nones, twelve moons, that is, twelve months, having passed, the birth of that same moon appeared.

IX. Accordingly the moon completes its year in three hundred and fifty-four days, but the sun in three hundred and sixty-five and a quarter; that is, there are eleven days and a quarter which the moon's reckoning seems, as it were, to have less than the sun's reckoning. [These are] the six days of the moon's hollowings, [made of] twelve halves, and those five which, in memory of God's workmanship, used to be called empty, which the Roman arrangement has now distributed over certain months, and which it called intercalary, and that quarter, which belongs rather to the reckoning of the sun; this quarter, reckoned in addition, making a whole [day] four times over through the passing of four years, is added to the sun's course as the bissextile [day] of the sixth before the Kalends of March. But since sun and moon, day and night, each have their reckoning bound up with the other, these eleven days and the bissextile quarter are added beyond the 353 days of the lunar year, and so the sun's year is known to have 365 days and a quarter. Therefore, since the moon completed its first year, that is, on the fifth day before the Nones of March, the third day before the Nones of March is seen to belong to the first month.

X. But since divine goodness has so ordained that the solemnity of Easter be celebrated, beyond doubt, in no other than the first month, for that reason we do not seek the first moon, for the reckoning of Easter, from the fourth day before the Nones of March; for on that day, as that very first year came round, the moon appeared not as a full whole but as a half, whereas on the other day, that is, the third before the Nones of March, it is known to have been first as a full whole. Hence we understand that it ought to take the increments of its whole, from its rising to its birth, only from the fourth day before the Nones of March, so that the third day before the Nones of March may more properly fall for us as the first [moon]. Now, therefore, when the first moon falls on the fourth day before the Nones of March, we pass it over for this reason: because that whole is completed in the twenty-four hours of night and day, and it begins its increment toward its whole from the day of the last month of the past year, which is the fifth day before the Nones of March, and [we pass it over] lest the first moon of the first month should seem to have the beginning of its increments in the last month. This fourth day before the Nones of March is kept by us as a middle day, to stand between the day of the last month that has passed and the third day before the Nones of March, so that the first moon which falls on the third day before the Nones of March may have the beginning of its increment from the fourth day before those same Nones. For on that day, that is, on the third before the Nones of March, if the first moon falls there, without any doubt about the year it is found to be first on a day of the first month, and it receives its increment toward its birth from a day of the first month.

XI. Therefore, from that day, the third before the Nones of March, to the fourth day before the Nones of April, we must seek where the first moon falls, because on whichever day of these twenty-nine the first moon falls, from there the first lunar month begins. And it is established by true reckoning that the fourteenth moon lawfully falls from the fifteenth day before the Kalends of April to the seventeenth day before the Kalends of May. Running on from here, where the most holy day of Easter falls, certainly in that same first month which the moon has brought forth, it is right to keep Easter rightly and without any omission. For so the Lord testifies on this matter in Exodus, and says: You shall keep the festival of the Passover; for seven days you shall eat unleavened bread, as I commanded you, at the time of the month of new things. For in it you went out of the land of Egypt (Exod. 23:15, according to the Septuagint). Likewise in Leviticus the Lord commanded, saying: In the first month, on the fourteenth of the month, between the evenings, [is] the Passover of the Lord, and on the fifteenth of this month the festival day of unleavened bread to the Lord (Lev. 23:5, 6, according to the Septuagint). Likewise in Numbers: The Lord spoke to Moses in the desert of Sinai in the second year of their departure from Egypt, in the first month, saying: Speak, and let the children of Israel make the Passover in its season; on the fourteenth day of the first month, at evening, you shall make it according to its times, according to its law, and according to its ordinance you shall make it. And Moses told the children of Israel to make the Passover in the desert of Sinai, and as the Lord commanded Moses, so the children of Israel did (Num. 9:1–5, according to the Septuagint). And a little after, the Lord commanded with a threat, saying: The man who is clean, and was not on a long journey, and has failed to make the Passover, that soul shall be destroyed from his people, because he did not offer the gift to our Lord in its season, and that man shall bear his sin (ibid., 13). Likewise in Deuteronomy Moses speaks to the people, saying: Keep the month of new things, and you shall make the Passover to the Lord your God, because in the month of new things you went out of the land of Egypt by night, and you shall sacrifice the Passover of the Lord to your God (Deut. 16:1, 2, according to the Septuagint). Also in the first book of Ezra it is written more plainly: And Josiah kept the Passover to the Lord in Jerusalem, and sacrificed the *phasec* [Passover] on the fourteenth moon of the first month at evening (1 Esdras 1:1, according to the Septuagint; Vulgate 2 Chron. 35:1).

XII. But why do we run through many [texts], when the same is recorded in all the sacred Scriptures, that the Passover must be celebrated in the first month? But this moon does not have this first month fixed and bounded, so that it always falls on the same [days]; rather [it has] the twenty-nine days we mentioned above, from the third day before the Nones of March to the fourth day before the Nones of April, in which, the first year from the making of the world having passed, it displayed its first month; so that when it is first on one of these days, from there it brings forth for us the first month. For this reckoning produces the embolismic and common years. For if ever in the twelfth month, before the third day before the Nones of March, the days of its year which we mentioned above being completed, that same moon appears as first, it must fill a thirteenth month and make an embolismic year. If, the year having been completed in its proper time, that is, on the days which are seen to belong to the first month, namely after its twelve months have passed, the first moon falls, a common year has been made. For these twenty-eight days show embolismic and common years thus. There are eleven days from the third before the Nones of March to the day of the Ides of the same [month]; if the first moon falls on these, since it will be seen to be born after twelve months, it shows that the past years were common, but it marks as embolismic the present ones, in which, being born, it makes the first month. There are eight days from the seventeenth day before the Kalends of April to the tenth day before the Kalends of April; if the moon appears as first on these, it signifies both the past and the present years as common. Then there are ten days from the eighth before the Kalends of April to the third day before the Nones of the same; if the first moon falls on these, it makes the past years embolismic and shows the present ones common. Common years have three hundred and fifty-four days each; for either the moon's reckoning has eleven days less than the sun's reckoning and makes a common year, or it exceeds it by ten and nine and makes an embolismic one.

XIII. Hence, year by year, because of this difference, the days of the moon's years do not seem to agree with the days of the sun, which completes its year in three hundred and sixty-five [days] and a quarter. Therefore we show this too, so that it may be plain to all that they have days equal to each other, and that from the beginning their courses have run in this order, and that the same moon has made up in the embolismic years the losses of the common years. Let us set out the reckoning of eight years, which is seen to be complete. In eight years, that is, the moon has five common years and three embolismic. So five times 354 make 1770, and three times 384 make 1152; together they make 2922 days. Then let us likewise gather into one the sum of the sun's eight years: eight times 365 and a quarter, 2922. Thus, then, the course of the sun and moon has come together with the days written above.

XIV. We have set out what the day of the world is, which God almighty established in creating light, and how the moon was made at the beginning of night, or where it unfolded its first year, and why the first moon is sought by us from the third day before the Nones of March, and from which days the fourteenth [moon] is to be found, and also the reckoning of embolismic and common years, for full instruction, so that our descendants too may run through this course of the moon with the days of Easter, running on through endless years, and may investigate future times more easily and truly, [finding] on which day before the Kalends or the Ides it would fall, which day or which moon could occur in the first month, so that this little work of ours may be set up for all without toil, since the true reckoning has been laid out above, and the days of Easter themselves may be known, each in its own time, without toil or the stumbling-block of falsehood, by the many who are in doubt or ignorance. For our Pascha is one thing, that of the Jews another. Indeed our sacrament is far different from theirs, and we do not celebrate the Pascha to the Lord as they do, as is shown by clear reasoning in the following passage.

XV. For in the fifteenth year of the reign of Tiberius Caesar the Lord Christ, when he was about thirty years old, came forward, beginning from the baptism of John. This the Evangelist testifies. He then preached for one year to the Jewish nation, to which he had come, and in that year he not only foretold that the kingdom of heaven was coming, but also, so that they might believe, showed himself plainly to be the Lord in mighty works, and this up to the sixteenth year of the reign of Tiberius Caesar, in which no longer a lamb from the sheep, as is customary at the Jewish feast, but the Lord Christ himself was sacrificed for us, so that we who believe might be set free not from Egypt but from the world and its vices. For in that year, as the reliability of the calculation shows and reason itself persuades, the same Lord Christ suffered on the fourteenth moon, the eighth day before the Kalends of April, on the sixth weekday. And on the third day, as the first weekday dawned, which comes after the Sabbath of the Jews, the Lord's day, that is, our sabbath and the true Pascha, on which the same Lord Christ, having conquered death, by rising sanctified our Pascha, that is, he made the passage of liberation of the living and the dead from the sentence of the old man, and there rose for those who fear the Lord and believe in Christ the true sun of righteousness, with healing in its wings. Hence we Christians today, in memory of our liberation, no longer as the Jews with a slain lamb and unleavened bread of fine flour and on any day whatever, but after the likeness of the resurrection of our same Lord, on the first weekday, that is, on the Lord's day, keeping from the law only the first month, which the moon produces by running through its numbers, as it is written: From the fourteenth, full at evening, until the twenty-first, in the unleavened bread of sincerity and truth, that is, in purity of mind, we celebrate the Pascha to the Lord.
EPILOGUE.

With God's favour we have run through and set out everything that had to be said concerning the reckoning of Easter. Let us now make an end here of our discourse; and we completed this laborious work on this day, the third before the Nones of March, after the fourth consulship of Arcadius and the third of Honorius. Therefore we warn those who hastened to receive these writings from us before they were corrected, that they should try to have the work corrected according to this arrangement; and for that reason we have now fixed to this reckoning both the day and the consuls, which we did not put at first, so that from now on anyone may know that this work is the corrected one.
Quintus Julius Hilarianus finished [this], and corrected it on the third day before the Nones of March, in the consulship of Caesarius and Atticus.
